7. Ending this Agreement

7.1 We may end this Agreement by giving You six months’ notice in writing. This Agreement will also end if We permanently remove all Our Apparatus from Your property.

7.2 You may end this agreement by giving Us not less than 18 months’ prior written notice in accordance with paragraph 31 of the Code if You intend to redevelop all or part of Your property and could not reasonably do so unless the agreement is ended and an alteration under Clause 6.1 above is not possible.

7.3 You may end this agreement by giving Us 18 months’ written notice under paragraph 31 of the Code if:

7.3.1 this Agreement ought to come to an end as a result of substantial breaches by Us of Our obligations under the Agreement; or

7.3.2 We have persistently delayed making payments due to You under the terms of this Agreement; or,

7.3.3 the prejudice caused to you by the continuation of this Agreement is incapable of being adequately compensated by money and the public benefit likely to result from the continuation of the Agreement does not outweigh the prejudice to You.

7.4 This Agreement will remain in force until the apparatus is no longer required unless terminated in accordance with the above.

8. Notices

8.1 The procedure for sending notices under this Agreement is set out in the Code. We will send notices in writing to Your address shown on page 2 of this agreement. You must send any notice in writing to Our address at page 2.

9. General

9.1 If any dispute arises between the parties concerning the interpretation of this Agreement, the parties will resolve that dispute by negotiations for a period of no more than 30 days. If the dispute is urgent or unresolved after 30 days, the dispute will be referred to a single arbitrator where the parties can agree on one, or otherwise to an arbitrator appointed by the President of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors on the application of either party, and in any case the Arbitration Act 1996 or any statutory amendment or re-enactment will apply to the reference.

9.2 This Agreement will be governed by the laws of England and Wales and the Parties agree to submit to the exclusive jurisdiction of the English and Welsh Courts.

9. Annex 2: Memorandum of Understanding between Openreach, the Country Land and Business Association and the National Farmers Union

9.1 BT Apparatus

Openreach Ltd (Openreach) is a legally separate, wholly-owned subsidiary within the BT Group and as such manages a significant amount of electronic communications apparatus, lines and structures (definitions as set out in Schedule 3A of the Communications Act 2003) in urban and rural areas. Openreach manages the network assets on behalf of British Telecommunications plc (BT plc). All contracts will be in the name of BT plc, but all engineers, surveyors and wayleaves team are Openreach people.

The Country Land and Business Association (CLA) and the National Farmers Union (NFU) are the representative organisations for those who own and manage the land and grant Openreach the relevant permissions to install and keep electronic communications apparatus on their land.

The agreement between the parties is called a wayleave agreement and it covers the rights and obligations of both parties in granting the permission for the installation of communications apparatus. The wayleave agreement reflects a balance of protections and obligations for both the landowner and operator under the Electronic Communications Code.

The following framework sets out the process which should be followed in an effort to avoid disputes when negotiating wayleaves or the ongoing management of existing electronic communications apparatus.

The parties hereby agree the following.

1. Working together - OFCOM Code of Practice

Openreach, the CLA and the NFU are working together to make the process for requesting access to land from landowners for the installation of our network equipment as smooth as possible. They will abide or engage with the Ofcom Electronic Communications Code of Practice (ECC). The ECC Code of Practice provides the overarching principles by which all parties will work together with the aim of enabling the efficient roll-out of high-speed broadband whilst taking into account the needs of landowners. The Memorandum of Understanding gives more detail about how the Openreach process works.

2. Survey

The first step is the survey stage. When new network is needed, Openreach begins by surveying existing network to establish the best way to provide service for customers. If additions to the network are required, the surveyor will identify what is required and the best position for it to be placed.

Should Openreach need to install new apparatus on private land, the surveyor will make all reasonable efforts to identify and contact the landowner to make them aware that Openreach are proposing to provide apparatus on their land. Openreach will contact the landowner to request a survey, or, if they are already in the area, they may ask to discuss the proposed route and wayleave whilst they are there, if this is convenient to the landowner. In simple situations, the surveyor may try to obtain a wayleave agreement with the landowner on site. However, the landowner has no obligation to sign on site, they can consider the proposal whilst Openreach prepare the wayleave application which details what is proposed and why, in more depth.

3. Planning

This is the stage where Openreach plans the network to provide service to customers.

Once a survey is completed it is then passed to the Openreach planner to review, and plan on internal systems. The survey will confirm whether a wayleave is needed.

If the planner identifies there is proposed apparatus on private land and the surveyor could not identify the landowner, the planner will look to find the landowner through various processes, for example, Land Registry. If a landowner is identified, the planner will create a wayleave with the proposed associated route plan, and the Openreach Wayleaves Team will send it to the landowner. No work will commence on private land until the wayleave (including the associated route plan) is agreed.

If Openreach is unable to identify the landowner, Openreach will undertake further investigations in the local area including attempting to speak to neighbours, placing advertisements in local shops or publications, and if this does not identify the owner, a letter of intent will be displayed at the site. In very rare cases, once the statutory process has been followed, Openreach may apply to the Court for permission to carry out the works proposed.

4. Wayleave

This is the stage where Openreach would contact the landowner with a wayleave application.

Prior to sending the landowner the wayleave application via post or email, Openreach will attempt to contact the landowner by telephone to discuss what a wayleave is and why they are asking their permission to install apparatus on their land.

11.5 Section 5: The Landowner’s Responsibilities

5.1 Our apparatus belongs to us at all times. You and anyone you are responsible for must avoid damaging our apparatus. If you or someone you are responsible for damages our apparatus you will be liable for the reasonable costs of repair subject to a maximum amount to be determined save in the case you accidentally damage an underground

cable which is laid at a depth less than the recommended industry standard4 or greater in the event of certain agricultural practices such as, ploughing. However, you will not be liable for any consequential losses unless you maliciously or wilfully damage the apparatus.

5.2 You may not, without our prior written consent, place, build or plant anything on your property which denies us reasonable access to or will interfere with our apparatus but this does not apply to pre-existing trees or other vegetation.

11.6 Section 6: Notices

6.1 Notices under this agreement should be those set out by Ofcom. We will send notices in writing to your address shown on page 1 of this agreement. You must send any notice in writing to our address at page 1.

11.7 Section 7: Dispute resolution

7.1 The parties shall attempt to resolve any dispute arising out of this agreement through negotiations between senior members of both parties who have authority to settle disputes.

7.2 If a dispute is not resolved by negotiation within 30 days of receipt of a written invitation from one party to the other to negotiate a dispute the dispute will be referred to a single arbitrator where the parties can agree one, or otherwise to an arbitrator appointed by the President of the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors on the application of either party, and in any case the Arbitration Act 1996 or any other statutory amendment or re-enactment will apply to the reference.

7.3 Nothing in this clause shall be construed as prohibiting a party from applying to a court.

11.8 Section 8: Termination of this agreement

8.1 We may end this agreement by giving you six months’ notice in writing. This agreement will also end if we permanently remove all our apparatus from your property.

8.2 You may end this agreement by giving us not less than 18 months’ prior written notice if you intend to redevelop all or part of your property and could not reasonably do so unless the agreement is ended and an alteration under Clause 4.11 above is not possible.

8.3 You may end this agreement by giving us 18 months’ written notice if:

this agreement ought to come to an end as a result of substantial breaches by us of our obligations under the agreement; or

we have persistently delayed making payments due to you under the terms of this Agreement; or

the prejudice caused to you by the continuation of this Agreement is incapable of being adequately compensated by money and the public benefit likely to result from the continuation of the Agreement does not outweigh the prejudice to you

8.4 This agreement will remain in force until the apparatus is no longer required unless terminated in accordance with the above.
